question: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:

In 2025, around 15 % of young people in Europe were classified as NEETs, meaning that they were not in education, employment or training.1 Lockdown and school closure policies during the COVID-19 pandemic compounded this problem, hindering access to education and reducing young people’s employment opportunities. Already in 2021, the World Bank spoke of a ‘lost generation’ as a result of learning losses and the loss of social interaction.2 NEETs do not contribute to tax revenues and often rely on social benefits. The cost to European countries is estimated at around EUR 153 billion per year. This represents around 1.2 % of the gross domestic product of the entire EU.3 Against a backdrop of demographic change, persistent economic weakness, rising unemployment, as well as advancing digitalisation, including artificial intelligence, this situation presents a ticking time bomb. 1.
What specific measures will the Commission take to solve this problem, which has so far been downplayed?
How will these millions of children and young people be integrated into training programmes and the labour market?
What percentage of NEETs in the EU are young people with a migrant background?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (1.9.2026) The main EU policy framework to support young people’s labour market integration and address the NEET (Not in education, employment or training) phenomenon is the Youth Guarantee. Created in 2013, it was reinforced in 20201 to respond to the rising youth unemployment figures caused by the COVID-19 crisis. Since 2013, the Youth Guarantee has helped more than 63 million young people in Europe. Member States implement the Youth Guarantee through a variety of measures. The Commission supports them in these efforts, e.g. by monitoring the implementation and facilitating the exchange of best practices. As announced in the Anti-Poverty Strategy, by 2027, the Commission will develop a toolkit to strengthen the links between the Child and Youth Guarantees. EU funds and other EU initiatives related to education, training and upskilling – e.g. the Union of Skills, Erasmus+, the European Solidarity Corps, the European Alliance for Apprenticeships, the ALMA initiative – also support young people in building skills and confidence and gaining work experience. As regards young people with a migrant background, the Action Plan on Integration and Inclusion 2021-20272 complements mainstream youth policies by addressing barriers to participation in education, training and employment. The 2025 mid-term3 review confirms that, despite progress, migrant young people continue to face disadvantages, including a higher risk of early school leaving and difficulties in accessing employment matching their skills. In 2025 the NEET rate4 (15-29) stood at 11%5. The trend has been decreasing since 2013 (16.1%) apart from a peak during the COVID-19 pandemic (13.8% in 2020). In 20246, the percentage of NEETs with a migrant background7 was approximately 16%.
